In the figure above, $∠POQ$ is a straight angle. Find $m∠QOS.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $∠POQ$ is straight, $m∠POQ={180}^{∘}.$ So by the angle addition postulate, we have

$$
m∠QOR+m∠ROP={180}^{∘}.
$$

Substituting the given expressions into the above, we can solve for $w$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(4w-{7}^{∘})+(6w-{13}^{∘}) & ={180}^{∘} \\ 10w-{20}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 10w & ={200}^{∘} \\ w & ={20}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know $w={20}^{∘},$ we can calculate $m∠ROP$ as follows:

$$
m∠ROP=6({20}^{∘})-{13}^{∘}={107}^{∘}
$$

Finally, since the angles $∠QOS$ and $∠ROP$ are vertical angles, they have the same measure:

$$
m∠QOS=m∠ROP={107}^{∘}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠3-m∠2 & ={122}^{∘}-{58}^{∘} \\  & ={64}^{∘}.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding an Unknown Angle by Combining Properties of Straight and Vertical Angles
canonical_examples.problem:
In the figure below, $\angle AOB$ is a straight angle. Determine $m \angle AOD.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14173512/assets/6eac6c11dcc513cdf896cdfaa9650689af1bf58afd147783d0bb1ca61dd3a324.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $\angle AOB$ is straight, $m\angle AOB = 180^\circ.$ So by the angle addition postulate, we have

$$
m\angle AOC + m\angle BOC = 180^\circ.
$$

Substituting the given expressions into the above, we can solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5x+{100}^{∘})+11x & ={180}^{∘} \\ 16x+{100}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 16x & ={80}^{∘} \\ x & ={5}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know $x=5^\circ,$ we can calculate $m \angle COB$ as follows:

$$
m \angle COB = 11(5^\circ) = 55^\circ
$$

Finally, since the angles $\angle AOD$ and $\angle COB$ are vertical angles, they have the same measure:

$$
m \angle AOD = m \angle COB = 55^\circ
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
In the diagram shown below, it is known that $m \angle 1 = 60^\circ$ and $m \angle 3 = 120^\circ.$ Determine the value of $m \angle 2 + m \angle 4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14173512/assets/1bc662904a52724fac28dc180f70088592ff4da181930c6607b1bb590b3ec188.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We have two pairs of vertical angles, and we know that vertical angles are congruent and therefore have the same measure. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠1=m∠2, \\ m∠3=m∠4.\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that $m \angle 1 = 60^\circ$ and $m \angle 3 = 120^\circ,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{60}^{∘}=m∠2, \\ {120}^{∘}=m∠4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠2+m∠4 & ={60}^{∘}+{120}^{∘} \\  & ={180}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
When two lines meet at a point, they create two pairs of opposite angles. The angles in each pair are called **vertical angles**.

Vertical angles are *always* congruent.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14173512/assets/0d5b2895ae18beb7242ef666af08e5b8e3490880de99aec8d993b02f31a9fcf4.png)

In the diagram above, $\angle 1$ and $\angle 3$ are vertical angles and are therefore congruent. 

Likewise, $\angle 2$ and $\angle 4$ are vertical angles and are therefore congruent. 

So, we have $\angle 1 \cong \angle 3$ and $\angle 2 \cong \angle 4.$
